{{Short description|Fictional book from the Sherlock Holmes book series}}
[[File:The Dynamics of An Asteroid.jpg|right|thumb|350px|The cover of ''The Dynamics of an Asteroid'', from the 2011 film ''[[Sherlock Holmes: A Game of Shadows]]''.]]
'''''The Dynamics of an Asteroid''''' is a [[fictional book]] by [[Professor Moriarty|Professor James Moriarty]], the implacable foe of [[Sherlock Holmes]]. The only mention of it in [[Arthur Conan Doyle]]'s original Holmes stories is in ''[[The Valley of Fear]]'' (written in 1914, but set in 1888) when Holmes says of Moriarty:<ref>
{{cite book
 |first=Arthur Conan |last=Doyle |author-link=Arthur Conan Doyle
 |year=1929
 |title=The Complete Sherlock Holmes Long Stories
 |page=409
 |publisher=Murray
 |place=London, UK
 |isbn=978-0-7195-0356-6
}}
</ref>
{{Blockquote|Is he not the celebrated author of ''The Dynamics of an Asteroid'', a book which ascends to such rarefied heights of pure mathematics that it is said that there was no man in the scientific press capable of criticizing it?}}

Participants in the "[[Sherlockian game]]", where [[Sherlock Holmes fandom|Sherlock Holmes fans]] elaborate on elements within Doyle's stories, have suggested other details about ''The Dynamics of an Asteroid''.

==Related real works==
In 1809, [[Carl Friedrich Gauss]] wrote a ground-breaking treatise<ref>
{{cite book
  |author=Gauss, C.F.  |author-link=Carl Friedrich Gauss
  |year=1809
  |title=Theoria motus corporum coelestium in sectionibus conicis solem ambientium
  |publisher=Friedrich Perthes and I.H. Besser
  |place=Hamburg, Germany
  |url=https://books.google.com/books?id=HjLOAAAAMAAJ&q=theoria%20motus&pg=PP1
  |via=Google Books
}}
</ref> on the dynamics of an asteroid ([[Ceres (dwarf planet)|Ceres]]). However, [[Gauss's method]] was understood immediately and is still used today.<ref>
{{cite journal
  |first1=Donald |last1=Teets
  |first2=Karen  |last2=Whitehead
  |date=April 1999
  |title=The discovery of Ceres: How Gauss became famous
  |journal=Mathematics Magazine
  |volume=72 |issue=2 |pages=83–93
  |doi=10.1080/0025570X.1999.11996710
 |jstor=2690592
}}
</ref>

Two decades before [[Arthur Conan Doyle]]'s writing, the Canadian-American dynamic astronomer [[Simon Newcomb]] had published a series of books analyzing motions of planets in the [[Solar System]].<ref>
{{cite book
  |last=Marsden |first=B. 
  |year=1981
  |article=Newcomb, Simon
  |editor-last=Gillespie |editor-first=C.C.
  |title=Dictionary of Scientific Biography
  |volume=10  |pages=33–36
  |place=New York, NY
  |publisher=Charles Screibner's Sons
  |isbn=0-684-16970-3
}}
</ref> The notoriously spiteful Newcomb could have been an inspiration for Professor Moriarty.<ref>
{{cite journal
  |last=Schaefer |first=B.E.
  |year=1993
  |url=http://adsabs.harvard.edu/full/1993JBAA..103...30S
  |title=Sherlock Holmes and some astronomical connections
  |journal=Journal of the British Astronomical Association
  |volume=103  |number=1 |pages=30–34
|bibcode=1993JBAA..103...30S
 }}
</ref>

In 1887, [[Henri Poincaré]]'s submission to the celestial mechanics contest of King [[Oscar II]] of Sweden investigated the [[three-body problem]], a theoretical basis of asteroid dynamics.  It was also hard to criticize, as both the jury ([[Karl Weierstrass|Weirstrass]], [[Gösta Mittag-Leffler|Mittag-Leffler]], and [[Charles Hermite|Hermite]], all top-notch mathematicians) and the author himself missed a fatal error in the submission (later corrected).<ref>{{cite web |title=From Order to Chaos: The Prize Competition in Honour of King Oscar II |url=https://www.mittag-leffler.se/about-us/history/prize-competition/}}</ref>

Another example of mathematics too abstruse to be criticized is the [[Srinivasa Ramanujan#Contacting British mathematicians|letters of Srinivasa Ramanujan]], sent to several mathematicians at the [[University of Cambridge]] in 1913.<ref>
{{cite book
  |author=Kanigel, R.
  |year=1991
  |title=The Man Who Knew Infinity: A life of the genius Ramanujan
  |page=168
  |publisher=Scribner
  |isbn=978-0-671-75061-9
  |title-link=The man who knew infinity
}}
</ref>  Only one of these mathematicians, [[G. H. Hardy]], even recognized their merit.  Despite being experts in the branches of mathematics used, he and [[John Edensor Littlewood|J. E. Littlewood]] added that many of them "defeated me completely; I had never seen anything in the least like them before."  It has taken over a century for this work to be understood; the last sub-field<ref>{{cite book |author=Watson, G. N. |chapter=The final problem: an account of the mock theta functions |title=Ramanujan: essays and surveys |year=2001 |pages=325–34}}</ref> (and the last problem of the last sub-field<ref>{{cite journal |last1=Berndt |first1=Bruce C. |first2=Junxian |last2=Li |first3=Alexandru |last3=Zaharescu |title=The final problem: an identity from Ramanujan's lost notebook |journal=Journal of the London Mathematical Society |volume=100 n|issue=2 |year=2019 |pages=568–591 |doi=10.1112/jlms.12228 }}</ref>) have been referred to as [[The Final Problem]] in explicit reference to the Sherlock Holmes story.  Holmes only states that "it is ''said''" (emphasis added) that no one in the scientific press was capable of criticizing Moriarty's work; he stops short of recognizing the claim as indisputably accurate.

Similarly, when it was jocularly suggested to [[Arthur Eddington]] in 1919 that he was one of only three people in the world who understood [[Albert Einstein]]'s [[theory of relativity]], Eddington quipped that he could not think who the third person was.<ref>{{cite journal |last1=Chandrasekhar |first1=S. |authorlink=Subrahmanyan Chandrasekhar |title=Verifying the Theory of Relativity |journal=Notes and Records of the Royal Society of London |date=1976 |volume=30 |issue=2 |page=255 |jstor=531756 |issn=0035-9149}}</ref>

==Discussion of possible book contents==
Doyle provided no indication of the contents of ''Dynamics'' other than its title. Speculation about its contents published by later authors includes:

* "[[The Ultimate Crime]]", short story by [[Isaac Asimov]], in ''[[More Tales of the Black Widowers]]'',<ref>
{{cite book
 |author=Asimov, I. 
 |year=1976
 |title=More Tales of the Black Widowers
 |publisher=Doubleday
 |isbn=978-0-385-11176-8
 |url=https://archive.org/details/moretalesofblack00asim
}}
</ref> and republished in ''Sherlock Holmes through Time and Space''.<ref>
{{cite book
 |first1=I.   |last1=Asimov 
 |first2=C.G. |last2=Waugh
 |year=1985
 |title=Sherlock Holmes through Time and Space
 |pages=339–355
 |publisher=Severn House
 |place=UK
 |isbn=978-0-312-94400-1
}}
</ref>
* "The Dynamics of an Asteroid", short story by [[Robert Bloch]], ''[[The Baker Street Journal]]'', 1953, and also found in ''The Game is Afoot''.<ref>
{{cite book
 |editor-last=Kaye |editor-first=Marvin 
 |year=1994
 |title=The Game is Afoot
 |pages=[https://archive.org/details/gameisafootparod00kaye/page/488 488–493]
 |publisher=St Martin's Press
 |place=USA
 |isbn=978-0-312-11797-9
 |url=https://archive.org/details/gameisafootparod00kaye
 |url-access=registration
}}
</ref>
* "The Adventure of the Russian Grave", a short story by [[William Barton (writer)|William Barton]] and [[Michael Capobianco]], collected in ''Sherlock Holmes in Orbit''.<ref>
{{cite book
 |editor1-last=Resnick   |editor1-first=Mike 
 |editor2-last=Greenberg |editor2-first=Martin H. 
 |year=1997
 |title=Sherlock Holmes in Orbit
 |publisher=Fine Communications
 |isbn=978-0-886-77636-7
}}
</ref>
* In the novel ''[[Spider-Man]]: The Revenge of the [[Sinister Six]]'', by [[Adam-Troy Castro]], a veiled reference is made to Moriarty and his ''Dynamics''. Here the work is said to still be the authority on orbital bombardment.
* Physicist [[Alejandro Jenkins]] in 2013 suggested [[chaos theory]], an esoteric branch of mathematics whose association with asteroid dynamics was not appreciated by real-world mathematicians until the work of [[Henri Poincaré]] in 1890.<ref>
{{cite arXiv
 |last=Jenkins  |first=Alejandro
 |year=2013
 |title=On the title of Moriarty's '' 'Dynamics of an asteroid' ''
 |eprint=1302.5855
 |class=physics.pop-ph
}}
</ref><ref>
{{cite journal
  |last=Poincaré  |first=Jules Henri  |author-link=Henri Poincaré 
  |title=Sur le problème des trois corps et les équations de la dynamique. Divergence des séries de M. Lindstedt
  |journal=Acta Mathematica
  |volume=13  |issue=1–2  |pages=1–270
  |year=1890
  |doi=10.1007/BF02392506  |doi-access=free
}}
</ref><ref>
{{cite book
  |last1=Diacu  |first1=Florin
  |last2=Holmes |first2=Philip
  |year=1996
  |title=Celestial Encounters: The origins of chaos and stability
  |publisher=[[Princeton University Press]]
}}
</ref>
* [[Simon P. Norton]] and [[Alain Goriely]] have each suggested that the book might have been Moriarty's submission to the 1887 celestial mechanics contest<ref>{{cite book |last1=Stubhaug |first1=Arild |title=King Oscar's Prize |date=2010 |pages=377–380 |doi=10.1007/978-3-642-11672-8_43 |isbn=978-3-642-11671-1 |url=https://link.springer.com/chapter/10.1007/978-3-642-11672-8_43}}</ref> of King [[Oscar II]] of Sweden (which was won by [[Henri Poincaré]].)<ref>{{cite news |title=Sherlock Holmes and the Three-Body Problem |author= |magazine=Mathematics Today |date=February 2014 |publisher=Institute of Mathematics & its applications|citeseerx= 10.1.1.672.4223}}</ref><ref>{{cite news |title=The Mathematics Behind Sherlock Holmes: A Game of Shadows |author=Alain Goriely and Derek E. Moulton |magazine=SIAM News |volume=45 |issue=3 |date=April 2012 |publisher=Society for Industrial and Applied Mathematics |url=http://goriely.com/wp-content/uploads/2012-SIAM-News.pdf }}</ref>

===Related references in media===
* A different Sherlock Holmes story, [[The Final Problem]], mentions another mathematical paper by Moriarty - "[[A Treatise on the Binomial Theorem|a treatise on the binomial theorem]]".  It was written when Moriarty was only 21&nbsp;years of age.
* In "[[His Last Vow]]", the final episode of series 3 of the BBC television series ''[[Sherlock (TV series)|Sherlock]]'', Sherlock's mother, M.L. Holmes, is shown to have written a lengthy textbook with the title ''The Dynamics of Combustion'', a reference to this book.
* In "Henny Penny the Sky Is Falling", the 100th episode of the CBS television series ''[[Elementary (TV series)|Elementary]]'', the plot evolves around a fictional paper with the title ''Miscalculating Near-Earth Asteroids and the Threat to Human Existence''.
* The pastiche novel ''[[Professor Moriarty: The Hound of the D'Urbervilles]]'' by [[film critic]] and [[Horror (genre)|horror]] novelist [[Kim Newman]] includes a chapter parodying both "[[The Adventure of the Red-Headed League]]" and [[H. G. Wells]]'s novel ''[[The War of the Worlds]]'', in which an arrogant former student of Moriarty's named Nevil Airey-Stent publicly rubbishes ''The Dynamics of an Asteroid'' to prove that it is indeed susceptible to criticism, prompting an enraged Moriarty to orchestrate an elaborate plan to drive Stent insane by convincing him that he has been contacted by visitors from the planet [[Mars]].
* In the 2017 mobile game ''[[Fate/Grand Order]]'', Moriarty's Noble Phantasm is called ''The Dynamics of an Asteroid''. During the Shinjuku Pseudo-Singularity, his goal is to destroy the Earth following the theory developed in this book using the asteroid [[101955 Bennu]] as the "bullet," and the abilities of the Phantom Spirit of [[Freischütz|der Freischütz]] to guarantee it will destroy the Earth.
